background: Dual sourcing is a classic supply-chain model where a firm can replenish from a slow cheap supplier and a fast expensive supplier. The model is simple to state but hard because orders placed today arrive after different deterministic lead times, so the state includes a multi-period pipeline from each supplier. When the lead-time difference is one, the dynamic program has much more tractable structure. When the gap is two or more periods, the exact optimal policy has resisted a clean characterization for decades. This makes the problem a good fit for ORdős Problems: the modelling choices are already settled, the objective is a standard infinite-horizon inventory cost, and there are strong heuristic and asymptotic policies. Xin and Goldberg gave theoretical support for Tailored Base-Surge policies by proving asymptotic optimality when the regular-source lead time grows while the express-source lead time is fixed. That result resolves an important large-lead-time question, but it does not characterize the exact finite-lead-time optimal policy. The remaining open problem is structural: describe the optimal policy, or prove sharp non-asymptotic guarantees for a simple policy class, when the two lead times differ by at least two.
open_problem: For the fixed periodic-review average-cost model and lead-time gap at least two, prove an exact structural characterization of optimal replenishment decisions beyond an unrestricted full-pipeline dynamic program.
known_results:
Consecutive lead times admit order-up-to structure. For larger gaps, the optimal decision generally depends on the outstanding-order pipeline. Linwei Xin and David A. Goldberg prove asymptotic optimality of tailored base-surge (TBS) policies as the regular lead time grows with the expedited lead time fixed.

Poulad Moradi, Melvin Drent, Joachim Arts, and Collin Drent, arXiv:2207.12182v2 (October 2, 2026), extend the projected expedited inventory position (PEIP) theory. Under finite nonzero demand variance, Theorems 5.7 and 5.9 give exponential-in-gap cost comparisons and optimality-gap bounds with other parameters fixed. Theorem 6.3 gives relative asymptotic optimality when backlog penalty and expedited premium grow at a fixed ratio below the lead-time gap, subject to Assumption 6.2 on cumulative-demand tails. The latter requires bounded cumulative demand or sublinear conditional mean excess; finite variance alone is not the stated condition.

Remaining open problem. Characterize exact optimal policies for fixed finite lead-time gaps. Asymptotic guarantees and good numerical performance do not imply exact optimality at moderate parameters.

where_posed.text: The long-standing finite-gap structural problem is discussed in the dual-sourcing inventory literature; Xin and Goldberg identify the model as having resisted exact solution for more than forty years while resolving the large-regular-lead-time TBS asymptotic question.
where_posed.location: Introduction and model discussion of Xin and Goldberg 2016.

progress.summary: The October revision adds PEIP guarantees in long-lead-time and high-service regimes; fixed-parameter exact structure remains unresolved.

counterexample_rationale: Small finite lead-time and finite-demand-support instances can refute conjectured threshold or index structures through dynamic programming. A full characterization must handle an unbounded inventory/pipeline state.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can map optimal actions in truncated dynamic programs, infer switching surfaces, and locate counterexamples to proposed structures. It is less suited to proving asymptotic or infinite-state optimality without analytic support.

literature.synthesis: TBS deliberately simplifies the regular pipeline, whereas projection policies use it to control expected future inventory positions. Comparing these policies gives rigorous performance guarantees, but does not establish that a chosen heuristic is exactly optimal at fixed parameters.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Begin with two- or three-period lead-time gaps and finite-support demand, compute truncated Bellman equations, and look for monotone comparative statics or switching-curve regularity. Analytic approaches may use L-convexity, pipeline-state aggregation, vanishing-discount limits, or lower bounds tied to lost-sales/queueing asymptotics.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed exact policy must be checked against Bellman optimality for the specified infinite-horizon average-cost problem with explicit state variables. A claimed non-asymptotic guarantee must state the parameter regime and compare to the true optimal policy, not only to another heuristic.

short_statement: Two suppliers trade replenishment speed against cost. New guarantees support projection policies, while exact optimal control at a fixed lead-time gap remains poorly understood.
full_statement:
A single product is reviewed in discrete periods under i.i.d. nonnegative demand of finite positive mean and finite variance. Orders placed before demand arrive after deterministic lead times $L_r>L_e\ge0$ from an uncapacitated regular supplier and an expedited supplier. There are no fixed order costs. Unit prices satisfy $c_e>c_r$; unmet demand is fully backlogged, and end-of-period net inventory $I_t$ incurs $h(I_t)^++b(-I_t)^+$, with $h,b>0$.

A nonanticipating policy chooses nonnegative orders $(q_t^r,q_t^e)$ from current net inventory and outstanding orders. Under the long-run expected average-cost criterion, minimize $$J(\pi)=\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T(c_rq_t^r+c_eq_t^e+h(I_t)^++b(-I_t)^+)\right].$$ Fix an initial state with finite inventory and finite outstanding orders.

For a fixed lead-time gap $L_r-L_e\ge2$, characterize an optimal policy beyond the general full-pipeline Bellman formulation: identify and prove usable structural restrictions or sufficient statistics. A policy optimal only as a parameter diverges does not answer the finite-parameter question. Any algorithmic hardness assertion must specify an input representation rather than infer hardness from a large state space.
